name: Ahisamach
title: Father of Oholiab, from the tribe of Dan
summary: Ahisamach belonged to the tribe of Dan and is known exclusively from the Bible as the father of Oholiab – the gifted craftsman whom God appointed together with Bezalel to lead the construction of the tabernacle in the wilderness. Although Ahisamach has no independent story attached to him, he is named four times in Exodus as a patronymic identifier for his son. His lineage is nevertheless significant: through Oholiab, Ahisamach's name was permanently linked to the holy mission of building the sanctuary where God would dwell among the people of Israel. That this central craftsman came from Dan, one of the less prominent tribes, underscores that God calls and equips people regardless of social status.
roles: Man from the tribe of Dan

keyEvents.title: Oholiab appointed as craftsman for the tabernacle
keyEvents.description: God chose Oholiab, son of Ahisamach from the tribe of Dan, together with Bezalel to lead the work of constructing the tabernacle and all its equipment.

keyEvents.title: Oholiab given ability to teach
keyEvents.description: Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, was given wisdom from God not only to perform craftwork but also to teach others the necessary skills.

keyEvents.title: Work on the tabernacle begins
keyEvents.description: Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, worked alongside Bezalel and other skilled craftsmen whom God had given wisdom and understanding to carry out the construction of the sanctuary.

keyEvents.title: Oholiab mentioned in the overview of the tabernacle's construction
keyEvents.description: In the summary of the completion of the tabernacle, Oholiab, son of Ahisamach from the tribe of Dan, is identified as an engraver, craftsman, and embroiderer.

versions.summary: Ahisamach was from the tribe of Dan and was the father of Oholiab, one of the leading craftsmen appointed by God to build the tabernacle in the wilderness. He is known through his son Oholiab's role in constructing the sanctuary. Ahisamach is mentioned several times in Exodus as a way of identifying Oholiab's lineage.

versions.reason: [minor] Ahisamach was not himself a craftsman in the tabernacle – he is only known as the father of Oholiab. The title should reflect this more precisely.; [major] The roles array is empty. Although Ahisamach is primarily known as the father of Oholiab, he should have at least one role identifying him, for example 'Father of Oholiab' or 'Man from the tribe of Dan'.; [major] Exodus 37:29 concerns Bezalel's work with the anointing oil and incense, and Oholiab is not specifically mentioned in this verse. It is Bezalel who is the subject in chapter 37. This event should either be removed or corrected.; [minor] The summary states that Ahisamach is a 'Craftsman in the tabernacle', but the text itself clarifies that he is only known through his son. There is some contradiction. The summary should clarify that Ahisamach himself has no documented role beyond being Oholiab's father.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1400 BC' fits with a late dating of the Exodus from Egypt, but some scholars date it to c. 1446 BC or c. 1250 BC. A slightly broader formulation such as 'c. 1400s BC' may be more neutral.; [minor] Exodus 36:1-2 mentions Bezalel and Oholiab, but verse 1 mentions them together with other skilled men. The reference is correct, but the description 'engraver, artist, and embroiderer' belongs more to Exodus 38:23 than to 36:1-2.

versions.summary: Ahisamach was from the tribe of Dan and is known as the father of Oholiab, one of the leading craftsmen appointed by God to build the tabernacle in the wilderness. Ahisamach has no independently described role in the Bible but is repeatedly mentioned in Exodus as a way of identifying Oholiab's family background. Through his son, his name became linked with the holy work of constructing the sanctuary where God would dwell among His people.

footnotes.text: The name Ahisamach (Hebrew: אֲחִיסָמָךְ, 'Achisamakh') likely means 'my brother has supported' or 'brother of support,' composed of the roots אָח ('ach', 'brother') and סָמַךְ ('samakh', 'to support'). This is a typical Hebrew family name expressing gratitude for a brother's help and support.

The tribe of Dan had its inheritance in southwestern Canaan, along the coastal plain. The fact that one of the leading craftsmen at the tabernacle came from Dan highlights that artistic talent was not limited to specific tribes but was given by God's Spirit across tribal boundaries.

Oholiab's craftsmanship—engraving, intricate weaving, and embroidery—reflects techniques well known from Egypt and the ancient Near East. Archaeological finds from Egypt's New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE) testify to advanced textile work and metal engraving that correspond with the skills described in connection with the construction of the tabernacle.

In Jewish tradition (Midrash), Oholiab was seen as a parallel to Bezalel: Bezalel was from Judah, the most honored tribe, while Oholiab was from Dan, one of the least esteemed tribes. The rabbis interpreted this as an expression of the principle that God regards both great and small equally in His service (cf. Tanchuma, Ki Tisa 13).

In the biblical text, Ahisamach is mentioned exclusively as a patronym—meaning as a father's name to identify Oholiab. Such patronymic identification was very common in ancient Israel and throughout the Semitic cultural area, serving as a means to place individuals within their family and tribal context.
